glossary.Uric acid: A breakdown product of purines; too much forms crystals in gout and uric acid stones.
glossary.Dehydration: Too little water in the body, which concentrates urine and favours stones.
glossary.Oxalate: A substance in foods such as spinach and tea that binds calcium to form stones.
glossary.Groin: The area where the thigh meets the lower abdomen.
glossary.Tachycardia: A heart rate over 100 beats per minute.
glossary.Flank: The side of the body between the ribs and the hip.
glossary.Red flag: A feature that suggests a serious problem needing urgent action.
glossary.Microscopic haematuria: Blood in the urine seen only on dipstick or microscope, not by eye.
glossary.Alkaline urine: Urine with a high pH, which favours struvite stones.
glossary.Acidic urine: Urine with a low pH, which favours uric acid stones.
glossary.Decompression: Relieving the pressure in a blocked kidney by draining it with a stent or nephrostomy.
glossary.Calcium phosphate: A radiopaque stone type made of calcium and phosphate.
glossary.Ground-glass: A hazy, frosted appearance; here describing cystine stones.
glossary.Gout: Inflammatory arthritis caused by uric acid crystals in the joint.
glossary.Chemotherapy: Drugs used to kill cancer cells.
glossary.HIV: Human immunodeficiency virus, treated with antiretrovirals such as indinavir.
glossary.Non-contrast: A scan done without injected dye.
glossary.Pregnancy test: A urine or blood hCG test, done to exclude ectopic pregnancy in women with abdominal pain.
glossary.Blood cultures: Blood samples incubated to grow bacteria, used when sepsis is suspected.
glossary.U&Es: Urea and electrolytes: a blood test of kidney function and salts.
glossary.Ultrasound: An imaging test using sound waves, safe in pregnancy.
glossary.Watchful waiting: Monitoring without treatment, as small stones often pass on their own.
glossary.Alpha-blocker: A drug that relaxes smooth muscle, such as tamsulosin, helping stones pass down the ureter.
glossary.Shockwave lithotripsy: Breaking a stone into fragments with shockwaves applied through the skin.
glossary.Percutaneous nephrolithotomy: Keyhole removal of a large stone through a track made directly into the kidney.
glossary.Renal failure: Loss of kidney function so severe that waste and fluid build up.
glossary.AKI: Acute kidney injury: a sudden fall in kidney function over hours to days.
glossary.Hydrochlorothiazide: A thiazide diuretic that lowers urinary calcium to prevent stones.
glossary.Indapamide: A thiazide-like diuretic used to prevent calcium stones.
glossary.Bendroflumethiazide: A thiazide diuretic used to reduce urinary calcium and stone recurrence.
glossary.Aggregation: Crystals clumping together into a larger stone.
glossary.Ammonia: An alkaline gas made when urease splits urea, raising urine pH.
glossary.Magnesium ammonium phosphate: The chemical name for struvite stones.
glossary.Purine: A building block of DNA and RNA; its breakdown makes uric acid.
glossary.Cell lysis: Cells bursting open, releasing their contents such as purines.
glossary.Peristaltic: Wave-like muscle contractions that push contents along a tube.
glossary.Dermatomes: Areas of skin supplied by a single spinal nerve.
glossary.T11-L2: The spinal segments whose nerves supply the ureter, so pain is referred to the loin and groin.
glossary.Referred: Of pain: felt away from its source because the two areas share a nerve supply.
glossary.Distal convoluted tubule: The part of the nephron after the loop of Henle, where thiazides act.
